questions.text: What kind of version control system is Git?
questions.explanation: Background / Scenario: the lab explores “the fundamentals of the distributed version control system Git.” Each person has a full copy of the repository locally.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to set the name and email Git attaches to your commits.
questions.code:
devasc@labvm:~$ git config ___ user.name "SampleUser"
devasc@labvm:~$ git config ___ user.email sample@example.com
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2b: git config --global user.name "SampleUser" and git config --global user.email sample@example.com. --global applies them to every repository for this user.

questions.text: Fill in the option that lists your Git settings at any time.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2c: git config --list reviews the settings.

questions.text: In Part 2, the name and email you configure can be anything, but in Part 7 you reset them to match your GitHub account.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2b note: the settings can be anything at this point, but when you reset these global values in Part 7, you use your GitHub username. (Part 7, Step 7c: change them if they don't match your GitHub credentials.)

questions.text: Fill in the command that turns the current directory (git-intro) into a Git repository.
questions.code:
devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/git-intro$ git ___
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/devasc/labs/devnet-src/git-intro/.git/
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2f: git init initializes the current directory as a Git repository.

questions.text: After git init, where is the repository's change history kept?
options: In the hidden .git directory inside the project
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2f: the local repository lives in the hidden directory .git — “This is where all of your change history is located.”

questions.text: Why doesn't a plain ls show the .git directory, and what does the lab use instead?
options: Names starting with a dot are hidden; ls -a shows them
It's a system file; sudo ls shows it
It's only created on the first commit; git log shows it
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2f: .git is hidden, and you can see it with ls -a, which lists . .. .git.

questions.text: What does git status show in a brand-new, empty repository?
options: On branch master, No commits yet, and nothing to commit
A list of every file in the home directory as untracked
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/master'
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step 2g: you're on branch master, there are no commits yet, and there's nothing to commit — “create/copy files and use "git add" to track”. Checked by running git init and git status.

questions.text: You create DEVASC.txt but haven't run git add. How does git status list it?
options: Under Changes to be committed as new file
Under Changes not staged for commit as modified
It doesn't list it until you commit
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2: Git finds the new file but knows it isn't tracked, listing it under “Untracked files” with the hint to use git add <file>.

questions.text: Fill in the command that stages DEVASC.txt.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: git add DEVASC.txt stages the file.

questions.text: What is staging?
options: An intermediate phase before committing that snapshots the file's contents at the time of git add
Permanently saving the file into the repository's history
Creating a new branch for the file
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: staging is an intermediate phase prior to committing with git commit. It snapshots the file's contents when git add runs.

questions.text: After running git add, any further edits to the file are automatically included in the next commit.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: git add snapshots the contents at that moment, so “any changes to the file require another git add command prior to committing the file.”

questions.text: Once DEVASC.txt is staged (before the first commit), how does git status show it?
options: new file: DEVASC.txt under Changes to be committed
modified: DEVASC.txt under Changes not staged for commit
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3b: the staged change is displayed as “new file: DEVASC.txt” under “Changes to be committed”, with the hint git rm --cached <file> to unstage.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to commit the staged file with a message.
questions.code: devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/git-intro$ git ___ ___ "Committing DEVASC.txt to begin tracking changes"
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 4: git commit -m "...". The -m switch adds a message explaining the changes you've made.

questions.text: In [master (root-commit) b510f8e], what is b510f8e?
options: The commit ID — the first 7 characters of the commit's SHA1 hash
A random number that changes every time you run git log
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 4: every commit is identified by a unique SHA1 hash, and the commit ID is the first 7 characters of it. Your commit ID will differ from the lab's.

questions.text: Which command shows all commits in the current branch's history, with each commit's hash, author, date and message?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 5: git log shows the commit hash, then the author's name and email, the date and the commit message.

questions.text: Which echo command adds a line to the end of DEVASC.txt without erasing what's already there?
options: echo "I am beginning to understand Git!" >> DEVASC.txt
echo "I am beginning to understand Git!" > DEVASC.txt
echo "I am beginning to understand Git!" | DEVASC.txt
echo "I am beginning to understand Git!" < DEVASC.txt
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 1a: use >> to append to the existing file. A single > overwrites it.

questions.text: After appending a line to the already-committed DEVASC.txt, how does git status describe it?
options: modified: DEVASC.txt under Changes not staged for commit
new file: DEVASC.txt under Changes to be committed
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 2: Git already tracks the file, so the change shows as “modified” under “Changes not staged for commit”. It has to be staged again with git add (Step 3) before committing.

questions.text: In git log, the oldest commit is listed first.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 5a: “The latest commit is shown first.” 9f5c4c5 (“Added additional line to file”) is above b510f8e.

questions.text: Fill in the command that compares the original commit with the latest one.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 5b: git diff <commit ID original> <commit ID latest>.

questions.text: In the git diff output, what does the line starting with + mean?
questions.context:
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 I am on my way to passing the Cisco DEVASC exam
+I am beginning to understand Git!
options: That line was added to the file in the later commit
That line was removed in the later commit
That line was changed but not committed
That line has a merge conflict
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step 5b: the + sign followed by the text indicates the content that was appended to the file.

questions.text: Why does the lab recommend working on a branch instead of updating master directly?
options: So changes happen in another area without affecting master, preventing accidental updates that overwrite existing code
Because Git won't let you commit to master
Because branches are pushed to GitHub automatically
Because commits on branches don't need messages
questions.explanation: Part 5 intro: branching lets you make changes in another area without affecting the master branch, which helps prevent accidental updates that might overwrite existing code.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to create a branch named feature and then switch to it.
questions.code:
devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/git-intro$ git ___ feature
devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/git-intro$ git ___ feature
questions.explanation: Part 5, Steps 1 and 3: git branch feature creates the branch; git checkout feature switches to it.

questions.text: In this git branch output, what does the * mean?
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 2: the * next to master indicates the current branch — the one that is “checked out”. Creating feature doesn't switch to it.

questions.text: Right after committing on feature, git log shows these labels. What do they tell you?
questions.context:
commit cd828a7... (HEAD -> feature)
    Added a third line in feature branch
commit 9f5c4c5... (master)
    Added additional line to file
options: feature is checked out and one commit ahead; master still points at the previous commit
Both branches now contain the third line
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 6b: HEAD -> feature marks the working branch and its new commit; “The prior commit was done within the master branch”, which hasn't moved.

questions.text: You're on master. Fill in the command that pulls the feature branch's history into it.
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 8b: git merge <branch-name> — the branch name is the branch whose history is pulled into the current branch.

questions.text: Why did merging feature into master say Fast-forward?
options: master had no new commits since feature branched off, so Git just moved master forward to feature's commit
Git skipped the merge because nothing changed
The merge was done without checking for conflicts
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 8b output. master was still at 9f5c4c5, the commit feature started from, so Git simply moved it up to cd828a7 with no merge commit. Checked by replaying the lab's commands.

questions.text: Fill in the option that deletes the merged feature branch.
questions.code:
devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/git-intro$ git branch ___ feature
Deleted branch feature (was cd828a7).
questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 9b: git branch -d <branch-name>. Afterwards git branch lists only * master.

questions.text: When does a merge conflict happen?
options: When overlapping changes were made to a file and Git can't merge them automatically
Whenever two branches have different commit IDs
When the branch being merged has been deleted
questions.explanation: Part 6 intro: a merge conflict is when you have made overlapping changes to a file and Git cannot automatically merge them. Here, both branches changed the word “Cisco” on the same line.

questions.text: What does sed -i 's/Cisco/NetAcad/' DEVASC.txt do?
options: Replaces “Cisco” with “NetAcad” directly in the file
Prints the file with “Cisco” replaced, leaving the file unchanged
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 4: sed changes the word “Cisco” to “NetAcad”. s/old/new/ substitutes, and -i edits the file in place, so cat then shows “NetAcad”.

questions.text: Fill in the option that stages every modified tracked file and commits it in one command.
questions.code: devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/git-intro$ git commit ___ -m "Change Cisco to NetAcad"
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 6: git commit -a -m "..." stages and commits in a single command.

questions.text: git commit -a also stages and commits brand-new files you haven't added yet.
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 6: “The -a option only affects files that have been modified and deleted. It does not affect new files.” Confirmed by creating a new file before git commit -a: it stayed untracked.

questions.text: test changed “Cisco” to “NetAcad” and master changed it to “DevNet”, both committed. What happens on git merge test from master?
options: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in DEVASC.txt — the automatic merge fails
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 11: “Auto-merging DEVASC.txt / CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in DEVASC.txt / Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.” Reproduced by replaying the lab's commands.

questions.text: Match each conflict marker in DEVASC.txt to what it means.
questions.context:
<<<<<<< HEAD
I am on my way to passing the DevNet DEVASC exam
=======
I am on my way to passing the NetAcad DEVASC exam
>>>>>>> test
I am beginning to understand Git!
This text was added originally while in the feature branch
allChoices: Start of the current branch's (master's) version
End of the incoming test branch's version

pairs.match: Start of the current branch's (master's) version
End of the incoming test branch's version

questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 12b: the HEAD version (master, “DevNet”) sits between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======; the test branch's version (“NetAcad”) sits between ======= and >>>>>>> test. Step 12a's git log shows HEAD is master.

questions.text: To resolve the conflict and keep master's “DevNet” line, which lines does the lab delete with dd in vim? (Choose all that apply.)
options: I am on my way to passing the DevNet DEVASC exam
I am on my way to passing the NetAcad DEVASC exam
questions.explanation: Part 6, Steps 13–14: deleting the three marker lines and the NetAcad line leaves “I am on my way to passing the DevNet DEVASC exam”, “I am beginning to understand Git!” and the feature-branch line — exactly what cat shows afterwards.

questions.text: How do you save your changes and quit in vim?
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 13c: press ESC, then type : followed by wq (write and quit) and press Enter. :q! quits without saving; dd deletes a line.

questions.text: After you fix the conflict and commit, git log shows a Merge: line on the new commit. What does it list?
options: The two parent commits that were merged — master's and test's
The two branches that are still checked out
questions.explanation: Part 6, Step 16: 72996c0 is master's “Changed Cisco to DevNet” commit and b6130a6 is test's “Change Cisco to NetAcad” commit; the merge commit has both as parents. (Its message in the lab's log, “manually merged from branch test”, doesn't match the “Manually merged from test branch” typed in Step 15.)

questions.text: Git requires a central server or cloud service like GitHub to work.
questions.explanation: Part 7 intro: “Git runs locally and does not require any central file server or cloud-based hosting service.” GitHub helps when working within a team, as a central repository everyone updates.

questions.text: Which Git hosting services does the lab name? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Part 7 intro: popular Git services include GitHub, Stash from Atlassian, and GitLab. The lab uses GitHub because it's readily accessible.

questions.text: In cp ../DEVASC.txt ., what do .. and the final . mean?
options: .. is the parent directory; . is the current directory, keeping the same file name
.. is the home directory; . is the root directory
.. copies hidden files; . ends the command
.. is the current directory; . is the parent directory
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 6a: “The two periods and a slash prior the file name indicates the parent directory. The space and period following the file name indicates to copy file in the current directory with the same file name.”

questions.text: The local devasc-study-team directory must have the same name as the GitHub repository.
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 4b: “The directory does not have to match the name as the repository.” The link is made by git remote add, not the folder name.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to add the GitHub repository as a remote named origin.
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 8a: git remote add origin <URL> adds the Git URL as a remote alias; “origin” points to the new GitHub repository. The username in the URL is case-sensitive.

questions.text: Which command verifies the remote, listing its fetch and push URLs?
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 8b: git remote --verbose shows origin with its URL twice — once for (fetch) and once for (push).

questions.text: In the new devasc-study-team repository, before any commit, what does git log print?
options: fatal: your current branch 'master' does not have any commits yet
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 8c: the error indicates there are no commits. Copying DEVASC.txt copies only the file, not git-intro's history.

questions.text: What does “working tree clean” mean in git status?
options: Nothing has changed since the last commit — there's nothing new to report
The repository has been pushed to GitHub
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 10b: Git has compared your file listing to what you've told Git, and “it's a clean slate with nothing new to report.”

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to send the master branch to the GitHub remote.
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 11: git push origin master sends the commits to GitHub; the output ends with * [new branch] master -> master.

questions.text: When git push asks for your GitHub password, what do you enter?
options: A Personal Access Token with the “repo” scope
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 11: GitHub needs a Personal Access Token instead of your account password, generated at your profile's token settings page with full “repo” scope.

questions.text: If git push fails with “repository not found” because you typed the wrong URL, which command removes the bad remote so you can add it again?
questions.explanation: Part 7, Step 11 note: you most likely submitted an incorrect URL, and you reverse the git remote add with git remote rm origin.

questions.text: Match each command to what it does.
allChoices: Stages a file for the next commit
Records the staged changes with a message
Shows which files are untracked, modified or staged
Lists the branches and marks the current one
Pulls another branch's history into the current one

pairs.match: Stages a file for the next commit
Records the staged changes with a message
Shows which files are untracked, modified or staged
Lists the branches and marks the current one
Pulls another branch's history into the current one

questions.explanation: Parts 3–6: git add stages, git commit -m commits with a message, git status reports file states, git branch lists branches with * on the current one, git checkout switches, and git merge pulls a branch's history into the current branch.
